'''Francis David Peat'''<ref>''Science, Order, and Creativity'', by David Bohm and F. David Peat, 1987, Bantam Books, front matter (British Library Cataloguing in Publication Data)<!-- ISSN/ISBN needed --></ref> (18 April 1938 –6 June 2017) was a British [[Holism in science|holistic]] [[physicist]] and [[author]] who has carried out research in [[solid state physics]] and the foundation of [[Quantum mechanics|quantum theory]].

He was director of the [[Pari Center for New Learning]], which is located in the village of [[Pari, Civitella Paganico|Pari]] near [[Grosseto]] in [[Tuscany]], [[Italy]]. He was adjunct professor at the [[California Institute of Integral Studies]] and [[Schumacher College]], a [[Fellow]] of the [[World Academy of Art and Science]] and a Distinguished Fellow at the [[University of South Africa]].

== Biography ==
Peat was born in [[Waterloo, Sefton|Waterloo]], England in 1938.

Peat did his undergraduate studies at the [[University of Liverpool]]. There he received a [[PhD]] in physics in  1964. In 1965, he became [[assistant professor]] at [[Queen's University at Kingston|Queen's University]] in [[Kingston, Ontario]]. Subsequently, from 1967 to 1975, he worked as research scientist for the [[National Research Council of Canada]]. During this time, from 1971 to 1972, he performed a sabbatical study with [[David Bohm]] and [[Roger Penrose]] at [[Birkbeck College]] in London.<ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20170506072206/http://www.fdavidpeat.com/biography/resume.htm David F. Peat, curriculum vitae], Homepage of F. D. Peat (from the Internet Archive, 6 May 2017).</ref>

For many years he was associated with physicist and philosopher David Bohm; the two wrote the book ''[[Science, Order, and Creativity]]'' together, and Peat later wrote Bohm's [[biography]], ''Infinite Potential: The Life and Times of David Bohm''. In the context of this biography, Peat emphasized how Bohm had worked intensely on finding a mathematical expression for his vision of an interconnected, enfolded ''implicate order'', from which an ''explicate order'', the world of classical physics unfolds. Bohm also aimed at re-introducing time as a dynamic entity. According to Peat, the use of the term ''Bohmian mechanics'' for his theory "would have shocked Dave [Bohm] somewhat": what was happening with the ideas of Bohm's and [[Basil Hiley]]'s theory, similarly as what had occurred with those of [[Hermann Grassmann|Hermann Grassmann]], [[William Rowan Hamilton]] and [[William Kingdon Clifford]] before, was that physicists left the fundamental ideas aside and merely made use of them as an easy manner of performing calculations.<ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20161018092109/http://www.fdavidpeat.com/interviews/wie.htm Look for Truth - No Matter Where It Takes You], Interview of F. David Peat by Simeon Alev (from Internet Archive, 18 October 2016). Originally published in: ''What is Enlightenment?'' Spring/Summer 1997, Volume 6, Number 1.</ref>

While living in [[Canada]], Peat organized discussion circles between Western scientists and [[American Indian elder|Native American elders]], together with [[Leroy Little Bear]]<ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20160809010633/http://www.fdavidpeat.com/pcnl/faculty.htm Pari Center for New Learning: Faculty] (from the Internet Archive, 9 August 2016).</ref> who later obtained the 2003 National Aboriginal Achievement Award, now the [[Indspire Awards]], for Education. While living in London, Peat organized a conference between artists and scientists. In 1996 he moved from Canada to [[Pari, Civitella Paganico|Pari]], Italy.<ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20100616174816/http://learningtogive.org/resources/folktales/interviews/Hegedus_Peat.asp Fetzer Institute: David Peat] (from the Internet Archive, 16 June 2010).</ref>

In 2000, he founded the ''Pari Center for New Learning'', a center dedicated to education, learning and research, together with writer and researcher Maureen Doolan.<ref>[http://www.paricenter.com/biographies/doolan.php Maureen Doolan], biography, Pari Center</ref> The activities of the Pari Center comprise residential courses and conferences and possibilities for scholars and researchers to spend extended periods as residents in Pari.<ref>[http://www.paricenter.com/center/ The Center], website of the Pari Center. Accessed 10 April 2024.</ref>

Peat wrote on the subjects of science, art, and spirituality and proposed the notions of creative suspension and gentle action. He authored or co-authored many books including ''Synchronicity: The Bridge between Matter and Mind'', ''Seven Life Lessons of Chaos'', ''Turbulent Mirror'', ''Gentle Action'', and ''Pathways of Chance''. His most recent book was ''A Flickering Reality: Cinema and the Nature of Reality''.{{cn|date=April 2024}}

Peat died in 2017 at [[Pari, Civitella Paganico]], Italy.

== Gentle action ==
A focus of Peat's recent work was the concept of ''gentle action''. This approach, as envisaged by Peat, emphasizes a certain manner of action that is aimed at creating change in an effective manner. The approach calls for tolerating uncertainty yet suspending action at its onset in order to allow an overall view to emerge. It emphasizes the value of small-scale, [[Iteration#Project management|iterative]] actions compared to large, single-step interventions.<ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20150908202402/https://www.csh.umn.edu/wsh/prod/groups/ahc/%40pub/%40ahc/%40csh/%40wsh/documents/asset/ahc_asset_147218.pdf Gentle Action: A Better Way. Building a Basis for Action], by F. David Peat and John Miller (from the Internet Archive, 8 September 2015).</ref> In his book of the same name, published 2008, Peat points out connections of his approach to earlier concepts, emphasizing the importance of [[active listening]] and a similarity to the concept of [[wu wei]].

Peat's ''gentle action'' has been cited together with [[Otto Scharmer]]'s [[Theory U]] and [[Arnold Mindell]]'s worldwork as approaches by which individuals, groups, organisations and communities can deal with [[complexity|complex]] issues.<ref>Stefanos Michiotis: [http://www.inderscience.com/search/index.php?action=record&rec_id=34676 ''Public dialogue and strategic planning using methods based on complexity and archetypes''], International Journal of Decision Sciences, Risk and Management 2010, vol.&nbsp;2, no.&nbsp;1/2, pp. 129–145, {{doi|10.1504/IJDSRM.2010.034676}}, p. 142.</ref>

Learning modules based on Peat's ''gentle action'' approach have been put in place, among others, at the [[University of Minnesota]] and at [[Siena Heights University]].{{Citation needed|date=March 2017}}
